blocks.text: 1. overview
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443902616-950350944.png

Apriori, the previous topic, requires one full pass over the entire transaction database for every single itemset size it considers, a cost that compounds quickly on large datasets with many frequent itemsets of increasing size. FP-Growth, short for Frequent Pattern Growth, was built specifically to eliminate this repeated scanning cost. Rather than scanning the database once per itemset size, FP-Growth compresses the entire transaction database into a compact tree structure using just two total scans, then mines frequent itemsets directly from that in-memory tree, with no further database scans required at all.

This makes FP-Growth substantially faster than Apriori on large transaction datasets, often by a wide margin, while discovering exactly the same set of frequent itemsets in the end. It achieves this through two key ideas worth understanding in depth: a compact, shared-prefix tree structure for representing the transaction data efficiently, and a recursive, divide-and-conquer mining strategy that avoids Apriori's explicit candidate generation step entirely.
2. Just Two Scans of the Database

blocks.alt: Just Two Scans of the Database
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443902617-610782994.png

FP-Growth begins with a first scan through every transaction in the database, counting how often each individual item appears overall, exactly the same first step Apriori performs to find frequent 1-itemsets. Items that fail to meet the minimum support threshold are discarded entirely, and the remaining frequent items are sorted by descending overall count.

A second scan then passes through every transaction one more time. For each transaction, only its frequent items are kept, arranged in that same descending-frequency order, and this sorted, filtered item sequence is inserted into the tree structure covered in the next section. Critically, this is the only other pass required over the raw transaction data; everything after this point, discovering frequent itemsets of every size, happens entirely by working with the compact tree already built in memory, never revisiting the raw transactions again.
3. The FP-Tree
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443902619-821814029.png

The FP-Tree is a compact, shared-prefix tree built from the sorted, frequent-items-only version of every transaction. Each path traced from the root of the tree downward represents one or more transactions, and crucially, transactions that happen to share a common prefix of frequent items, once sorted into that consistent descending-frequency order, share the very same path through the tree, rather than each being stored as an entirely separate, redundant list.

This path-sharing is what gives the FP-Tree its compactness: real transaction data very often has many transactions sharing common frequent items, and the tree captures that shared structure directly rather than storing every transaction's full item list independently. Alongside the tree itself, a header table keeps track of every distinct frequent item and links together every occurrence of that item scattered across different branches of the tree, making it possible to quickly find every path involving a particular item without having to search the whole tree from scratch.
4. Building the Tree
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443902619-574520452.png

Building the FP-Tree happens incrementally, one transaction at a time, during the second database scan. For each transaction, its frequent items are already sorted by descending overall frequency, and this sorted sequence is inserted into the tree starting from the root. At each step, if a child node already exists at the current tree position matching the next item in the sequence, that existing path is simply followed and its count incremented by one, reflecting that one more transaction has now passed through that exact point in the tree.

If no matching child node exists yet, a brand new node is created for that item, with its count starting at one, and a new branch begins from that point. This process, checking for an existing matching child and either following it or creating a new one, repeats for every item in every transaction's sorted, frequent-item sequence, gradually building up the full, compressed tree structure as the second scan proceeds through the entire database.
5. Conditional Pattern Bases
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443902620-706528420.png

Once the full FP-Tree is built, finding frequent itemsets involving a specific item works through a technique called the conditional pattern base. Using the header table, every tree path that leads to a particular item, jam for example, can be located quickly. Extracting just the prefix portions of those paths, everything that comes before jam on each of those paths, produces jam's conditional pattern base, essentially a smaller, focused transaction set representing everything that co-occurs with jam.

From this conditional pattern base, a smaller conditional FP-Tree is built, following exactly the same tree-building process already described, just applied to this narrower, jam-specific dataset rather than the full original transaction database. Mining this much smaller conditional tree recursively then reveals every frequent itemset that includes jam alongside other items, without ever needing to revisit the original, much larger transaction database again.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This recursive conditional-tree construction repeats for every frequent item, and for combinations of items as the recursion goes deeper, systematically uncovering frequent itemsets of every size, entirely through tree operations rather than database scans.

blocks.text: 6. A Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443902620-178689008.png

FP-Growth's overall mining strategy is a genuine divide-and-conquer approach, standing in sharp contrast to Apriori's generate-and-test cycle covered in the previous topic. Rather than repeatedly generating candidate itemsets across the entire database and testing each one, FP-Growth breaks the overall mining problem down into many smaller, largely independent sub-problems, one per item, each working only with that item's much smaller conditional pattern base and conditional FP-Tree.

Because each of these sub-problems operates on a conditional tree that is typically far smaller than the original full transaction database, mining them is correspondingly much faster than repeatedly scanning and filtering the full original dataset the way Apriori does at every itemset size. This divide-and-conquer decomposition, splitting one large mining problem into many small, focused ones, is the structural reason FP-Growth achieves its substantial speed advantage.
7. noCandidateGen

Perhaps the most fundamental structural difference between the two algorithms is worth stating directly. Apriori explicitly generates candidate itemsets at every size, builds them from surviving smaller frequent itemsets, and then counts each candidate against the transaction data to see if it clears the minimum support threshold, a generate-and-test cycle repeated at every level. FP-Growth never generates a single explicit candidate itemset at any point in its entire process.

Instead, frequent itemsets simply emerge directly from the structure of the tree paths and their conditional pattern bases as the recursive mining proceeds. This is not merely a more efficient way of pruning candidates, the way the Apriori Property helps Apriori; it eliminates the candidate generation step, and the combinatorial candidate explosion problem that comes with it, entirely, which is a structurally different, and generally faster, way of arriving at the same final set of frequent itemsets.
8. Speed in Practice
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443903200-629525211.png

Combining the benefits of just two total database scans, a compact shared-prefix tree representation, and the complete elimination of candidate generation, FP-Growth is typically dramatically faster than Apriori on real transaction datasets, particularly as the dataset grows large or as the number of frequent itemset sizes being mined increases. Benchmark comparisons between the two algorithms commonly show FP-Growth completing in a fraction of the time Apriori requires on the same data, sometimes by an order of magnitude or more.

This speed advantage tends to grow larger as the transaction database becomes denser, meaning transactions share more common frequent items, since a denser database produces a more compact FP-Tree relative to its size, giving FP-Growth's tree-sharing advantage more room to pay off. On sparse transaction data, where few transactions share common items, the FP-Tree compresses the data less effectively, and the speed gap between the two algorithms tends to narrow somewhat, though FP-Growth still generally holds an advantage.

blocks.text: 9. Choosing Between Apriori and FP-Growth

For genuinely small datasets, or in settings where tracing exactly how each candidate itemset was generated and tested matters for interpretability or teaching purposes, Apriori's explicit, step-by-step generate-and-test process can actually be easier to follow and explain than FP-Growth's more intricate recursive tree-based mining. On small data, the performance difference between the two rarely matters in any practical sense anyway.

For any dataset of meaningful size where speed genuinely matters, FP-Growth is almost always the better practical choice, given its substantial and well-documented speed advantage. The one situation where Apriori might still be preferred despite its slower speed is when memory is severely constrained and even FP-Growth's compact tree structure cannot comfortably fit, since Apriori's per-pass processing has a simpler, more predictable memory footprint at any given moment, though this is a comparatively rare practical concern with modern hardware.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below runs FP-Growth on the same grocery transaction data used in the Apriori worked example, comparing the resulting frequent itemsets directly.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
import time
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, fpgrowth
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder

transactions = [
    ["bread", "butter", "jam"],
    ["bread", "butter"],
    ["bread", "milk"],
    ["bread", "butter", "jam", "milk"],
    ["butter", "jam"],
    ["bread", "butter", "milk"],
]

encoder = TransactionEncoder()
encoded_array = encoder.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)
df = pd.DataFrame(encoded_array, columns=encoder.columns_)

start = time.time()
apriori_itemsets = apriori(df, min_support=0.4, use_colnames=True)
apriori_time = time.time() - start

start = time.time()
fpgrowth_itemsets = fpgrowth(df, min_support=0.4, use_colnames=True)
fpgrowth_time = time.time() - start

print(f"Apriori found {len(apriori_itemsets)} itemsets in {apriori_time:.6f}s")
print(f"FP-Growth found {len(fpgrowth_itemsets)} itemsets in {fpgrowth_time:.6f}s")
print("\nBoth algorithms should find the exact same frequent itemsets:")
print(sorted(apriori_itemsets['itemsets'].astype(str)) == sorted(fpgrowth_itemsets['itemsets'].astype(str)))

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: On this tiny example dataset the timing difference is negligible, but the itemsets found by both algorithms are always identical, since both are exhaustively finding every itemset that clears the same minimum support threshold, just through structurally different search strategies.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: FP-Growth finds the same frequent itemsets as Apriori while needing only two total scans of the transaction database.
The FP-Tree compresses transactions into a shared-prefix tree, storing common patterns far more compactly than a flat list.
A header table links every occurrence of each item across the tree, enabling fast, targeted lookups.
Conditional pattern bases extract just the prefixes leading to a specific item, enabling focused, smaller-scale recursive mining.
FP-Growth uses a divide-and-conquer strategy, breaking mining into many small, per-item sub-problems on conditional trees.
Unlike Apriori, FP-Growth never generates explicit candidate itemsets; frequent itemsets emerge directly from tree structure.
This design typically makes FP-Growth substantially faster than Apriori on real transaction data, especially as it grows large.
Apriori remains useful for small datasets, interpretability, or severely memory-constrained situations.
